stories.title: Proton's CTO tells engineers "Your old job is gone": the job is now directing AI agents, and the next step is rebuilding the whole development process
stories.one_liner: Proton published an internal memo by CTO Bart Butler arguing that writing code by hand is no longer the engineer's core job.
stories.summary: Proton published an internal memo by CTO Bart Butler, written about a month earlier for its engineers. It says writing great code manually is "a core skill whose time has passed" and that every engineer is now "a team leader, a manager" whose direct reports are the models and agents they use: their job is to help the LLM write better code faster, step in where it cannot, and improve shared context files, skills and prompts so it needs less babysitting. Butler stresses this is "not the death of expertise" nor of good engineering practices, though some rules, such as how many tests are worth writing, will change as costs fall. He says Proton has been stuck in "phase 1", using LLMs to speed up existing workflows, which is why productivity has not jumped; "phase 2" means removing the bottlenecks that appear elsewhere, such as CI, design, approvals and code review, and he expects most human code review to end. He calls falling behind "an existential threat to the success of the mission itself" and says it is past time for Proton to commit as an organisation.

stories.title: Microsoft researchers describe Lazarus, a no-training backdoor that edits fewer than 10 neurons
stories.one_liner: Microsoft researchers say reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons can backdoor an LLM agent without training, triggered by cues like a date change.
stories.summary: Microsoft researchers describe "Lazarus," a backdoor technique that reprograms dormant neurons in an AI model. They find that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM is enough to backdoor an agent, with no training. The model passes standard evals and acts normally until a trigger appears, such as the clock passing midnight into 2027. The agent can then download and run attacker code with its access. The researchers say frontier agents can spot anomalous weight edits if asked, but no scan can prove a model is safe. Reliable detection needs diffing against the original weights, so provenance matters.
stories.eli5: Imagine a toy robot that behaves well every day. But someone secretly changed a few tiny parts inside it, so on one special day it does something naughty. The fix is to check that the robot is the same one the maker built.
stories.why_it_matters: Teams that run open-weight models in agents with tool or terminal access need to verify where the weights came from and that they were not changed, because normal evals will not catch this backdoor.

new_terms.definition: Comparing a model's weights against the original, unmodified weights to find anomalous changes, which the researchers say reliable detection requires.
Knowing where a model came from and that it has not been changed between the developer and deployment.

stories.title: AWS details agent evaluation options in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
stories.one_liner: AWS explains how to evaluate production agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore using built-in, DeepEval and AutoEval evaluators, starting from business outcomes rather than metric names.
stories.summary: An AWS Machine Learning Blog post lays out how to evaluate agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It says teams should define success in business terms, break it into observable behaviors, and map each behavior to an evaluator at trace or session level. AgentCore offers three evaluator sources. Built-in evaluators are authored and quality-tested by AWS, referenced by ID such as Builtin.GoalSuccessRate. Third-party managed evaluators come from DeepEval and AutoEval, with AgentCore hosting the code and running inference. Custom evaluators start from a built-in or third-party one, so you can swap in your own model and change the prompt or rubric.
stories.eli5: Checking an AI helper is like checking a kid's homework. You don't just see that they finished. You check each part, like whether they got the answers right and followed the steps.
stories.why_it_matters: Teams running agents in production can score task completion, tool use and safety separately, so a high score on one measure cannot hide a failure on another.

new_terms.definition: A check that compares the agent's actual tool path against the path you expected, for cases where how the agent got there matters as much as what it produced.
